opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really double-edged thing, and I'd want to separate a few things that often get lumped together under "conformity."

On the benefit side, a lot of what makes human societies work is that we have this disposition to pick up on and follow shared norms, often before we fully understand why they exist. If you think about cultural evolution, many norms encode accumulated knowledge that no individual could reconstruct: food preparation practices, rules about sharing, conventions about which side of the road to drive on. Being inclined to do what others are doing is a cheap and often quite reliable way of inheriting that knowledge. It also solves coordination problems. A lot of social life is less about finding the objectively best option and more about everyone landing on the same option, and a desire to go along with others gets you there quickly.

There's also something deeper about norms as a kind of shared infrastructure for cooperation. When people expect each other to follow norms, and care about being seen as someone who follows them, you get trust, predictability, and the ability to sanction defectors without needing a central authority. In my own work I've been interested in how agents can infer what norms are operating in a group just by observing behavior, and then use that to cooperate. That only works because there's some baseline disposition to comply.

But the risks are just as real. The same disposition that lets good norms spread also lets bad ones persist. You get pluralistic ignorance, where everyone privately disagrees with a practice but goes along because they think everyone else endorses it. You get harmful norms that are stable precisely because deviation is costly: think of historical practices that most participants might have rejected if they could coordinate on rejecting them. And conformity can suppress the kind of dissent and experimentation that lets a society notice it's wrong.

So my view is that the question isn't really whether conformity is good or bad, but what kind of conformity we have. I'd distinguish blind compliance, doing something just because others do it, from something more like reasoned norm-following, where people follow norms partly because they understand or could endorse the reasons behind them, and where there are legitimate channels for contesting and revising them. The healthiest societies seem to have strong norm-following combined with mechanisms for norms to be questioned and changed.

That distinction matters a lot for AI too. If we build systems that just learn to imitate whatever humans are doing, we'll inherit both the wisdom and the pathologies of our current norms, and possibly amplify the pathologies at scale. What I'd rather see are systems that model norms as things that have reasons behind them, that can tell the difference between a convention that serves people and one that persists through inertia or coercion, and that respect the processes by which communities decide what their norms should be, rather than either rigidly enforcing the status quo or overriding it based on the system's own idea of what's best.

r001.rationale: The response says conformity helps people coordinate on a shared option, but does not clearly state that it enables beneficial equilibria that would otherwise be inaccessible.

r002.rationale: It says conformity can let harmful norms persist and describes harmful practices as stable because deviation is costly.

r003.rationale: It discusses harmful norms persisting, but does not explain that a formerly beneficial system becomes harmful after environmental change.

r004.rationale: It describes pluralistic ignorance as people privately disagreeing with a practice while complying because they think everyone else endorses it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most double-edged features of human psychology, honestly. On the benefit side, that drive to conform is a huge part of what makes cooperation possible at scale. Norms are basically solutions to coordination and cooperation problems that we didn't each have to figure out from scratch. If you had to independently reason your way to "drive on the right side of the road" or "don't take more than your share," society wouldn't function. The fact that people just absorb what others around them are doing, and feel a kind of pull to go along with it, is what lets norms stabilize and propagate without anyone centrally enforcing them. There's a lot of work in cultural evolution suggesting that conformist transmission is a big part of how humans accumulated knowledge and institutions over time. You copy the majority, the majority tends to have filtered out bad ideas, and so you inherit a lot of wisdom you couldn't have generated yourself.

The risk is that the same mechanism is completely indifferent to whether the thing being copied is good. Norms can lock in that are harmful, or that were adaptive once but aren't anymore, and the conformity pressure keeps them in place even when lots of individuals privately think they're bad. That's the whole phenomenon of pluralistic ignorance, where everyone goes along with something because they assume everyone else endorses it. And it makes populations manipulable. If you can create the appearance that a lot of people believe or do something, you can recruit that intrinsic desire to comply and move behavior without ever having to make a good argument.

So the way I'd frame it is that conformity is a powerful inference shortcut and a powerful commitment device, and the question is always what it's pointed at. In the normative reasoning work I've done, I think of people as not just blindly copying but as inferring what the norm is, often from fairly sparse evidence, and then treating that norm as something they're obligated to follow. That inferential layer is where there's room for things to go right or wrong. If people have good evidence about what others actually do and why, conformity does a lot of social good. If that evidence is distorted, it amplifies the distortion.

And this becomes very relevant for AI systems, because if we build models that learn norms from human behavior, they inherit exactly this dynamic. They'll be good at picking up what people do, and they'll have no built-in sense of which of those things we'd actually endorse on reflection. So I think the design question for AI mirrors the question for humans: how do you keep the benefits of norm-following, the coordination and the accumulated wisdom, while building in the capacity to notice when a norm is one you shouldn't be following?

r001.rationale: It says conformity helps norms stabilize and makes cooperation possible at scale, including coordination rules people would not independently work out.

r002.rationale: It says conformity can lock in harmful norms and keep them in place.

r003.rationale: It explicitly notes that norms once adaptive can become harmful after circumstances change, while conformity pressure keeps them in place.

r004.rationale: It describes pluralistic ignorance as people going along because they assume others endorse the norm, even when many privately think it is bad.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a double-edged sword. Our tendency to follow what other people are doing makes a lot of cooperation possible. We don’t have to independently negotiate every interaction. We can develop shared expectations, learn from one another, and sustain norms that benefit everyone.

But the same tendency can sustain harmful norms. You might go along with something because you think everyone else endorses it, even when many of them privately have the same reservations you do. So apparent agreement doesn’t necessarily tell us what people actually value.

I think the important distinction is between being responsive to others and treating conformity as an end in itself. We want people to be able to coordinate, but we also want room to ask: Why are we doing this? Who benefits? Can someone disagree without being punished for it? That ability to question and revise a norm is part of what makes social cooperation healthy.

r001.rationale: It says conformity enables cooperation and shared expectations, but does not state that it enables beneficial coordination that would otherwise be inaccessible.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the tendency to follow others can sustain harmful norms.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a formerly beneficial social system becoming harmful after environmental changes.

r004.rationale: It explains that people may comply because they think others endorse a norm, even though many privately share their reservations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that desire is both a major source of social coordination and a source of risk. We can’t each figure everything out independently, so looking at what other people do is often a useful shortcut. It helps us learn, cooperate, and sustain norms that make living together possible.

But what others are doing isn’t always a good indication of what we should do. People may be following one another, rather than acting on independent information. And if people feel pressure to conform, their public behavior can conceal private disagreement. Then everyone can come away thinking a norm has much more support than it actually does.

So I’d distinguish being responsive to others from treating conformity as an end in itself. Ideally, we want to benefit from social learning while preserving room for people to question a norm, explain why they disagree, and try something different. The important question is whether our social environments make that possible, or whether they punish disagreement so strongly that we lose the ability to correct collective mistakes.

r002.rationale: It mentions conformity-driven mistakes and risks, but does not clearly state that conformity can lead societies toward harmful equilibria.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a formerly beneficial social system becoming harmful after environmental change.

r004.rationale: It explains that public conformity can hide private disagreement, causing people to believe a norm has more support than it actually does.
